\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{だす} (dasu)}{だす (dasu)}]{\ja{だす} (dasu) — to take out}

\label{lesson:JA-C31-dasu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for to lend, then the Japanese for to give back.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{だす}}
\textbf{\ja{だす}} — \emph{dasu} — \textquotedblleft{}to take out\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{だす}} (\emph{dasu}) is a native Japanese word, inherited rather than borrowed from Chinese, and its older origin is not settled. Its kanji was attached to it later as a kun'yomi, a native reading given to a Chinese character (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{ごはん} (gohan)}{ごはん (gohan)}]{\ja{ごはん} (gohan) — rice; a meal}

\label{lesson:JA-C31-gohan}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for to fix, then the Japanese for to move.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{ごはん}}
\textbf{\ja{ごはん}} — \emph{gohan} — \textquotedblleft{}rice; a meal\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{ごはん}} (\emph{gohan}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{go}, \textquotedblleft{}honourable; a polite prefix\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{ngjoH}) and \emph{han}, \textquotedblleft{}cooked rice\textquotedblright{} (\emph{bjonX}) (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese after Baxter–Sagart). The polite \emph{go-} is the on'yomi of the character whose native reading gives \emph{o-}.
\end{cousinweb}
